text: What is it about fentanyl that is so much more dangerous than, say, meth? Between 2020 and 2021, the rate of overdose deaths doubled in Idaho. I know it takes a while for public health and mortality data to process, but from what you’re seeing, are we on the same trajectory with that rate rising? Wills: What are Idaho State Police troopers seeing on the ground with fentanyl users and dealers? Do people you arrest understand how lethal and prevalent fentanyl is? (Are users aware of the risk, or ignorant?) The governor launched Operation Esto Perpetua last year. Is it effective so far? Wills: Gov. Little deployed troopers to the Texas/Mexico border for Operation Esto Perpetua, in part to learn about drug interdiction techniques. What did they bring back from that trip? State law currently doesn’t include fentanyl on the list of drugs that would carry a mandatory minimum for possession or dealing. A bill to change that failed during the last legislative session. Do you believe adding a mandatory minimum sentence for people convicted of fentanyl possession would help address the problem? -We didn’t see significant change when mandatory minimums were added for dealing other controlled substances, so why would this be different? (Historically, mandatory minimums just incarcerate more people, rather than stop drug use.) Hurwit: For those who aren’t familiar, what lands a case in your jurisdiction as opposed to state court? Your office recently prosecuted a Pocatello woman selling fentanyl, Hailey Card, and a man died of overdose from the fentanyl she was distributing. How has the rate of overdose with this drug changed the way prosecutors approach these prosecutions? Is this a philosophy that’s consistent across districts? Do you talk to other US attys about it? How does the prosecution of these major crimes, rather than just small-time dealers, affect your office’s prosecution load and federal prison capacity? Either: Counterfeit pills are becoming more common place. Someone may think they’re taking a painkiller like an Oxycodone or Vicodin tablet, but the pill has fentanyl in it. Students at UI are currently lobbying to make fentanyl test strips legal in Idaho so users can reduce risk of overdose. Where do you stand? Idaho lawmakers voted to limit who can get free Narcan kits to first responders, as opposed to family members or friends of people addicted to opioids, or users themselves. And these kits are expensive, making some doctors hesitant to prescribe it. Do you see any other avenues for making narcan more accessible to the general public? (If they mention the generic version coming out soon: The over-the-counter version of Narcan coming later this year will still cost $50 for two doses. For a lot of people and families, that’s a significant amount of money.) Are there any other strategies that can reduce the risk? Any policy changes you would like to see to reduce this threat?
